rows: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r

questions.question: Q1. State the laws of refraction.
questions.answer: (i) Incident ray, refracted ray and the normal are coplanar. (ii) Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ (ratio of sines is constant for a pair of media).
questions.example: From air (n=1) into glass (n=1.5) at 30°: sin r = sin30/1.5 = 0.333 → r ≈ 19.5°.

questions.question: Q2. Define refractive index of a medium.
questions.answer: Refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium: n = c/v. It also equals sin(angle in rarer)/sin(angle in denser) for the two media.
questions.example: Light in water travels at c/1.33 ≈ 2.25×10⁸ m/s.

questions.question: Q3. Find the angle of refraction for light entering water (n = 1.33) at 45° from air.
questions.answer: n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂ → 1×sin45 = 1.33 sin θ₂ → sin θ₂ = 0.707/1.33 = 0.532 → θ₂ ≈ 32.1°.

questions.question: Q4. Explain apparent depth of a pool.
questions.answer: An object underwater appears shallower than it really is because rays bend away from the normal emerging from the denser medium; the eye traces them back in a straight line, making the bottom look closer. Apparent depth ≈ real depth / n.
questions.example: A 1.33 m pool looks ~1 m deep.

questions.question: Q5. Two media have refractive indices 1.2 and 1.5. Find relative index of medium 2 w.r.t. 1.
questions.answer: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = 1.5/1.2 = 1.25 (light goes from 1 to 2 bends toward the normal). ▥ 15.1–15.2 Laws of Refraction & Refractive Index  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Reflection vs Refraction Absolute vs Relative Refractive Index ▣ 15.3 Lateral Shift

questions.question: Q6. Derive the lateral shift through a glass slab of thickness d.
questions.answer: A ray entering a slab at angle i, refracting to r, emerges parallel but laterally displaced. Lateral shift t = d·sin(i − r)/cos r.
questions.example: A thicker slab / larger i gives a bigger shift.

questions.question: Q7. A 5 cm thick glass slab (n=1.5) is hit at 45°. Find the lateral shift.
Q8. Why does a glass slab not disperse white light (chromatic) as a prism does?
questions.answer: The faces are parallel, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray with no net angular deviation; different colors suffer equal lateral shifts and recombine, so no color separation (a wedge/prism, not parallel faces, separates them). ▥ 15.3 Lateral Shift  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Apparent vs Real Depth in Refraction ▣ 15.4 Total Internal Reflection
questions.shortcut: Parallel faces → no net deviation → no dispersion.
questions.example: A prism has angled faces → white light splits into a spectrum.

questions.question: Q9. Define total internal reflection (TIR). State the two conditions.
questions.answer: TIR is the complete reflection of light back into a denser medium when it strikes the interface with a rarer medium. Conditions: (i) light travels from a denser to a rarer medium, and (ii) the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle i_c (sin i_c = 1/n).
questions.shortcut: denser→rarer AND i > i_c ; sin i_c = 1/n.

questions.question: Q10. Find the critical angle for glass-air (n = 1.5).
Q11. Explain the working of an optical fibre using TIR.
questions.answer: Core has a higher index than the cladding. Light entering at a small angle is totally internally reflected at the core-cladding boundary, bouncing down the fibre with very little loss, carrying information as light pulses.
questions.shortcut: n_core > n_clad; repeated TIR carries the signal.
questions.example: Fibers send high-speed data by TIR.

questions.question: Q12. Why does a diamond 'sparkle' more than a glass? (relation to critical angle.)
questions.answer: Diamond's high refractive index (≈2.42) gives a small critical angle (i_c ≈ 24°). A large fraction of light entering is TIR'd multiple times before exiting, increasing brilliance and sparkle. Cut facets are aligned with this.
questions.shortcut: Higher n → smaller i_c → more internal reflection.

questions.question: Q13. A swimmer is underwater looking up. Explain the 'circle of light' effect.
questions.answer: Only rays from within a cone (half-angle i_c) can escape the water to air; outside this cone TIR keeps them trapped. To the swimmer the world above appears as a bright circle (Snell's window) surrounded by TIR (the water's surface). ▥ 15.4 Total Internal Reflection  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Total Internal Reflection vs Ordinary Reflection PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: i_c ≈ 48.8° for water-air; world seen through a circular window.
questions.example: The window edges correspond to the critical angle.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the lateral shift through a glass slab of thickness d.
theoryItems.answer: A ray entering a slab at angle i, refracting to r, emerges parallel but laterally displaced. From the geometry, the lateral shift t = d·sin(i − r)/cos r, where r is found from Snell's law (sin r = sin i / n).
theoryItems.example: Thicker slab or larger i → larger shift.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the condition for total internal reflection and the critical angle.
theoryItems.answer: TIR occurs when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium (n_d > n_r) and the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle i_c where the refraction angle is 90°: sin i_c = n_r/n_d = 1/n (for air). Beyond i_c no ray is refracted — all light reflects internally.
theoryItems.shortcut: TIR: denser→rarer AND i > i_c ; sin i_c = 1/n.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. State the laws of refraction (Snell's law) and define refractive index.
theoryItems.answer: Laws: (i) incident, refracted and normal are coplanar; (ii) n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂ (constant ratio). Refractive index n = c/v (speed in vacuum / in medium) = sin θ_rare/sin θ_dense.
theoryItems.shortcut: n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂ ; n = c/v.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T4. Compare total internal reflection with ordinary (partial) reflection.
theoryItems.answer: Ordinary reflection at an air-water surface is partial (some refracts, some reflects) for any angle; TIR is total (nothing refracts) but only beyond the critical angle and only from the denser side. TIR is therefore lossless and used for guiding light.
theoryItems.shortcut: Partial at any angle; TIR total but i > i_c, denser side.
theoryItems.example: A prism can totally reflect where a surface only partly reflects.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain apparent depth and the refraction seen in a pool.
theoryItems.answer: A submerged object looks shallower because rays bend away from the normal emerging from the denser water; the eye traces them back straight, so the bottom appears closer: apparent depth = real depth / n. This is why a pool looks shallower than it is.
theoryItems.example: A 1.33 m pool looks ~1 m deep.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain total internal reflection and its applications (optical fibre, mirage, diamond).
theoryItems.answer: TIR lets light stay trapped in a denser medium (like the core of an optical fibre or the atmosphere near the ground). Optical fibres transmit data as light by repeated TIR; a mirage is TIR in the air gradient; a diamond's small critical angle gives intense internal reflection and sparkle.
theoryItems.example: n_core > n_clad keeps the light guided.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the working of an optical fibre.
theoryItems.answer: Light is launched into a high-index core; at the low-index cladding interface the angle exceeds i_c, so each incidence is a TIR bounce. The light propagates down the fibre with minimal loss, carrying information as pulses (or as in a medical endoscope).
theoryItems.shortcut: n_core > n_clad; repeated TIR carries the signal.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain a mirage as TIR in air (superior and inferior).
theoryItems.answer: Near hot ground the air temperature decreases with height, so the refractive index increases upward; light rays curve upward (continuous refraction ≈ TIR), forming an inferior mirage (a 'pool' below). In a cold inversion (superior), rays curve downward, giving a floating image above the surface (Fata Morgana).
theoryItems.shortcut: Temperature gradient → index gradient → curved rays.
theoryItems.example: Inferior mirage: a fake water pool on the road.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T9. Why does a diamond 'sparkle' more than a glass stone?
theoryItems.answer: Diamond's high refractive index (~2.4) gives a very small critical angle (~24°); a large fraction of entering light is TIR'd many times before exiting, and the facets are cut to favour this, giving intense internal reflection and colour sparkle. Glass has a larger i_c and scatters more.
theoryItems.shortcut: Higher n → smaller i_c → more TIR → sparkle.
theoryItems.example: The cut is aligned with the small critical angle.

▣ 15.1–15.2 Laws of Refraction & Refractive Index
Q1. State the laws of refraction.
Answer:  (i) Incident ray, refracted ray and the normal are coplanar. (ii) Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ (ratio of sines is constant for a pair of media).
⚡ Shortcut:  n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂ (Snell).
Example:  From air (n=1) into glass (n=1.5) at 30°: sin r = sin30/1.5 = 0.333 → r ≈ 19.5°.
Q2. Define refractive index of a medium.
Answer:  Refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium: n = c/v. It also equals sin(angle in rarer)/sin(angle in denser) for the two media.
⚡ Shortcut:  n = c/v ; air ≈ 1, water ≈ 1.33, glass ≈ 1.5.
Example:  Light in water travels at c/1.33 ≈ 2.25×10⁸ m/s.
Q3. Find the angle of refraction for light entering water (n = 1.33) at 45° from air.
Answer:  n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂ → 1×sin45 = 1.33 sin θ₂ → sin θ₂ = 0.707/1.33 = 0.532 → θ₂ ≈ 32.1°.
⚡ Shortcut:  θ₂ = sin⁻¹(sin θ₁ / n₂).
Example:  ≈ 32°.
Q4. Explain apparent depth of a pool.

Answer:  An object underwater appears shallower than it really is because rays bend away from the normal emerging from the denser medium; the eye traces them back in a straight line, making the bottom look closer. Apparent depth ≈ real depth / n.
⚡ Shortcut:  Apparent depth = real depth / n.
Example:  A 1.33 m pool looks ~1 m deep.
Q5. Two media have refractive indices 1.2 and 1.5. Find relative index of medium 2 w.r.t. 1.
Answer:  n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = 1.5/1.2 = 1.25 (light goes from 1 to 2 bends toward the normal).
⚡ Shortcut:  n_rel = n₂/n₁; n_rel > 1 → toward normal.
Example:  n₂₁ = 1.25, n₁₂ = 0.8.

Q6. Derive the lateral shift through a glass slab of thickness d.
Answer:  A ray entering a slab at angle i, refracting to r, emerges parallel but laterally displaced. Lateral shift t = d·sin(i − r)/cos r.
⚡ Shortcut:  t = d·sin(i−r)/cos r.
Example:  A thicker slab / larger i gives a bigger shift.
Q7. A 5 cm thick glass slab (n=1.5) is hit at 45°. Find the lateral shift.
⚡ Shortcut:  t = d·sin(i−r)/cos r.
Example:  ≈ 1.6 cm shift.
Q8. Why does a glass slab not disperse white light (chromatic) as a prism does?

Answer:  The faces are parallel, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray with no net angular deviation; different colors suffer equal lateral shifts and recombine, so no color separation (a wedge/prism, not parallel faces, separates them).
⚡ Shortcut:  Parallel faces → no net deviation → no dispersion.

▣ 15.4 Total Internal Reflection
Q9. Define total internal reflection (TIR). State the two conditions.

Answer:  TIR is the complete reflection of light back into a denser medium when it strikes the interface with a rarer medium. Conditions: (i) light travels from a denser to a rarer medium, and (ii) the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle i_c (sin i_c = 1/n).
⚡ Shortcut:  denser→rarer AND i > i_c ; sin i_c = 1/n.
Example:  Optical fiber works by TIR.
Q10. Find the critical angle for glass-air (n = 1.5).
⚡ Shortcut:  i_c = sin⁻¹(1/n).
Example:  ≈ 42°; larger i_c for lower index.
Q11. Explain the working of an optical fibre using TIR.

Answer:  Core has a higher index than the cladding. Light entering at a small angle is totally internally reflected at the core-cladding boundary, bouncing down the fibre with very little loss, carrying information as light pulses.
⚡ Shortcut:  n_core > n_clad; repeated TIR carries the signal.
Example:  Fibers send high-speed data by TIR.
Q12. Why does a diamond 'sparkle' more than a glass? (relation to critical angle.)

Answer:  Diamond's high refractive index (≈2.42) gives a small critical angle (i_c ≈ 24°). A large fraction of light entering is TIR'd multiple times before exiting, increasing brilliance and sparkle. Cut facets are aligned with this.
⚡ Shortcut:  Higher n → smaller i_c → more internal reflection.
Example:  Diamond i_c≈24° vs glass ~42°.
Q13. A swimmer is underwater looking up. Explain the 'circle of light' effect.

Answer:  Only rays from within a cone (half-angle i_c) can escape the water to air; outside this cone TIR keeps them trapped. To the swimmer the world above appears as a bright circle (Snell's window) surrounded by TIR (the water's surface).
⚡ Shortcut:  i_c ≈ 48.8° for water-air; world seen through a circular window.
Example:  The window edges correspond to the critical angle.
